etymology: A city in the inheritance of Benjamin; also the name of a mountain in the hill country of Ephraim from which King Abijah rebuked Jeroboam. The name is taken to mean “double fleece” or “two peaks.”
biblical_def: Zemaraim is a city in the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the roll of Benjamin’s towns: “And Betharabah, and Zemaraim, and Bethel” (Jos 18:22). The same name marks a mountain in the hill country of Ephraim, the scene of one of the great confessions of Scripture. When Jeroboam led the ten tribes in revolt and idolatry, King Abijah of Judah “stood up upon mount Zemaraim, which is in mount Ephraim” (2Ch 13:4), and cried out to the armies of the north the ground of Judah’s confidence: “behold, God himself is with us for our captain…O children of Israel, fight ye not against the LORD God of your fathers; for ye shall not prosper” (2Ch 13:12). Though outnumbered two to one, Judah cried unto the LORD and the priests sounded the trumpets, and God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah. So the mount of Zemaraim became a pulpit for the truth that the LORD Himself is the captain of His people, and that no host, however great, can stand against those with whom God fights. The believer’s cause is safe not by numbers nor by strategy but by the presence of the living God, who is a wall of fire round about His people and the glory in the midst of them.
webster_summary: A city of Benjamin, and a mountain of Ephraim where Abijah proclaimed that God Himself was Judah’s captain against Jeroboam.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the roll of Benjamin’s towns; the name is taken to mean “God heals” or “God will restore.”
biblical_def: Irpeel is a city in the inheritance of Benjamin, named once with its neighbors: “And Rekem, and Irpeel, and Taralah” (Jos 18:27). It is nowhere else mentioned and no deed of its people is recorded. Yet its name is a small sermon, for it is compounded of the name of God and a word meaning to heal or make whole — God heals. Among the towns of the promised land there stood a place that carried in its name the great mercy of the covenant God, Jehovah-rapha, the LORD that healeth. “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exo 15:26), He said to Israel at the bitter waters made sweet; and the psalmist blesses Him “who healeth all thy diseases” (Psa 103:3). This healing is more than of the body; it is the healing of the backsliding and the broken-hearted, the binding up of the wounds that sin has made. “He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds” (Psa 147:3). The obscure Benjamite town of Irpeel, God-heals, points forward to the great Physician, Christ, by whose stripes we are healed, and who came not to the whole but to the sick, to bind up the broken and to make the wounded soul whole again. The name outlasts the town: God still heals His people, in soul and at last in body, when this mortal shall put on immortality.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the roll of Benjamin’s towns; the name means “village of the Ammonites,” preserving in the inheritance a memory of the heathen nation.
biblical_def: Chephar-haammonai is a city in the inheritance of Benjamin, named once in the roll of its towns: “And Chepharhaammonai, and Ophni, and Gaba; twelve cities with their villages” (Jos 18:24). The name means village of the Ammonites, and it preserves, in the very map of the promised land, a memory of the heathen who had once dwelt there or ranged so far. Such names dotted Israel’s inheritance — a Village of the Ammonites here, a Tower of Fortune there — standing reminders that the land had been taken from the nations, and that the nations’ ways lay ever near at hand as a snare. The LORD had warned that the peoples not driven out would be thorns in Israel’s sides, “and their gods shall be a snare unto you” (Jdg 2:3). A town bearing the name of Ammon, whose god was Molech and whose worship was the burning of children, was a name to give Benjamin pause. It called the tribe to remember that they dwelt among relics of the heathen, and must not learn their ways nor serve their gods. So this obscure village preaches separation: the people of God dwell in a world still marked with the names and monuments of its old idolatries, and are called to be in it but not of it, keeping themselves unspotted, and pulling down in heart every high place the nations left behind.

etymology: A city in the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the roll of Benjamin’s towns; the name is uncertain, and is taken by some to mean “reeling” or “staggering.”
biblical_def: Taralah is a city in the inheritance of Benjamin, named once with its neighbors: “And Rekem, and Irpeel, and Taralah” (Jos 18:27). It is nowhere else mentioned, and no deed of its people is recorded. The name is uncertain, and is taken by some to carry the sense of reeling or staggering — the tottering of one who cannot stand firm. If so, the name preaches by contrast, for the whole burden of Scripture concerning the people of God is that they should not be moved. “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Psa 16:8). The wicked stagger like a drunken man and are tossed with every wind; but the righteous, rooted in Christ, are established and cannot be shaken. “He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved” (Psa 62:2). A Benjamite town whose name suggests reeling stands, then, as a quiet summons to steadfastness: to be rooted and built up in Christ, established in the faith, so that whatever storms beat upon the house, it falls not, being founded upon the Rock. The believer’s stability is not in himself, for in himself he totters, but in the LORD at his right hand, who upholds him that he shall not be moved for ever.

etymology: A place on the northern approach to Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin near Michmash and Gibeah; the name is taken to mean “precipice” or “landslip.”
biblical_def: Migron is a place on the northern approach to Jerusalem, in the land of Benjamin near Michmash and Gibeah. It appears twice in Scripture, each time at a moment of crisis. In the days of Saul, when the Philistines had gathered a great host and Israel was cowering in caves, “Saul tarried in the uttermost part of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree which is in Migron: and the people that were with him were about six hundred men” (1Sa 14:2). While the king sat idle beneath his tree, his son Jonathan went up alone with his armour-bearer against the garrison, saying, “there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” (1Sa 14:6), and God gave a great deliverance by the faith of one man. Long after, Isaiah pictures the terror of the Assyrian march sweeping down these same roads: “He is come to Aiath, he is passed to Migron; at Michmash he hath laid up his carriages” (Isa 10:28). So Migron is a place of contrasts: the seat of Saul’s idle unbelief, and a station on the road of judgment. It preaches that the LORD is not restrained by numbers, saving by few as easily as by many; and that the proud invader who sweeps past Migron is himself but a rod in God’s hand, to be broken when his appointed work is done.

etymology: A place near Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, named in Isaiah’s prophecy of the Assyrian march; the name is taken to mean “pits” or “trenches,” from the cisterns dug there.
biblical_def: Gebim is a place near Jerusalem, in the land of Benjamin, named a single time in Isaiah’s vivid prophecy of the Assyrian invasion, as the terror sweeps from town to town toward the holy city: “Madmenah is removed; the inhabitants of Gebim gather themselves to flee” (Isa 10:31). The name is taken to mean pits or trenches, perhaps from cisterns dug in that place. Isaiah paints the panic of the countryside: village after village emptied, the people gathering their goods to flee before the advancing host. Yet the prophecy does not end in terror. The very chapter that pictures the flight from Gebim promises that the LORD will lop the bough of Assyria with terror, and the high one shall be hewn down; and it declares the great hope of the remnant: “The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God” (Isa 10:21), no more to lean upon the arm that smote them, but to stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth (Isa 10:20). So the flight from Gebim is set within a larger mercy. God uses the invader to chasten and to sift, but preserves a remnant, and turns the fleeing people back at last to Himself. The believer reads in Gebim both the seriousness of divine chastening and the sure preservation of the elect remnant, whom no Assyrian can finally destroy.

etymology: A village of Benjamin on the road from Jerusalem toward the Jordan, east of the Mount of Olives; the name is taken to mean “young men’s village” or “chosen ones.”
biblical_def: Bahurim is a village of Benjamin on the road running east from Jerusalem toward the Jordan, over the shoulder of the Mount of Olives. It appears in the darkest passage of David’s life, his flight from his son Absalom. “And when king David came to Bahurim, behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera: he came forth, and cursed still as he came” (2Sa 16:5). Shimei flung stones and dust and railing at the fleeing king; and when Abishai would have slain him, David forbade it, bowing under the rod and leaving his cause with God. At the same Bahurim, God preserved David’s messengers, hidden in a well by a faithful woman when Absalom’s servants pursued them (2Sa 17:18). So this one village holds both a cursing and a hiding, both the malice of an enemy and the shielding hand of God. David’s meekness under Shimei’s curses is a bright foreshadowing of great David’s greater Son, “who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). Bahurim teaches the saint to bear reproach without revenge, leaving vengeance to the LORD, who says, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom 12:19), and who hides His own in the day of trouble.

etymology: A place in Judah where Samson slew a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of an ass; the name means “jawbone,” and the spring there was called En-hakkore, “the well of him that cried.”
biblical_def: Lehi is a place in Judah, the scene of one of the mightiest of Samson’s deeds. When the Philistines came up and spread themselves in Judah to seize him, “the Philistines went up, and pitched in Judah, and spread themselves in Lehi” (Jdg 15:9). There, the Spirit of the LORD coming mightily upon him, Samson took the fresh jawbone of an ass and slew a thousand men, and named the place Ramath-lehi, the lifting-up of the jawbone. The name Lehi means jawbone. Afterward Samson was “sore athirst, and called on the LORD” (Jdg 15:18), confessing that God had given this great deliverance by the hand of His servant, and pleading his need; and God clave a hollow place, and water came forth, and Samson revived, “wherefore he called the name thereof Enhakkore…which is in Lehi unto this day” (Jdg 15:19) — the well of him that cried. So Lehi holds together the strength and the weakness of the man of God: mighty in the Spirit’s power to slay a thousand, yet fainting for a cup of water, and taught by thirst to cry unto the LORD. The victory was God’s gift, and so was the reviving spring. The believer learns at Lehi that the same God who works great things through His servants also humbles them with need, that they may cry to Him and know the deliverance and the drink alike are His.

God works great things by His servants, then brings them low, that they may cry to Him and own the deliverance as His.
roots_summary: A place in Judah where Samson slew a thousand with a jawbone and God gave him water at En-hakkore, the well of him that cried.
roots_lines: Lehi — a place in Judah; the name means jawbone.

He named the place Ramath-lehi, the lifting-up of the jawbone.
Sore athirst, he cried to the LORD (Jdg 15:18).
God clave a spring, called En-hakkore, the well of him that cried (Jdg 15:19).
usage: At Lehi Samson slew a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of an ass.

The victory and the reviving drink were alike the gift of God.

etymology: A place toward the Jordan valley to which the Midianite host fled when Gideon’s three hundred routed them; the name means “house of the acacia” or “place of the acacia tree.”
biblical_def: Beth-shittah is a place toward the Jordan valley, named in the great rout of the Midianites by Gideon and his three hundred. When the trumpets blew and the pitchers were broken and the torches blazed in the night, “the LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Bethshittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath” (Jdg 7:22). The name means house of the acacia. The whole story of Gideon is a monument to the doctrine that salvation is of the LORD alone; for God had whittled Israel’s army from thirty-two thousand down to three hundred, saying, “The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me” (Jdg 7:2). So the flight of the Midianites past Beth-shittah was no victory of Israelite arms — three hundred men with trumpets and torches never struck a blow — but the direct act of God, who turned the enemy’s swords upon themselves. Beth-shittah preaches the gospel pattern: God saves by few and weak and unlikely means, emptying His people of every ground of boasting, that the glory of the deliverance may be wholly and confessedly His own.
webster_summary: A place toward the Jordan to which the Midianites fled from Gideon’s three hundred; a monument that salvation is of the LORD, not the arm of man.

The LORD set every man’s sword against his fellow throughout the host.
God had reduced Israel’s army to three hundred, lest they boast.
The rout was God’s act, that the glory might be wholly His.

etymology: A city beside Zaretan, on the Jordan, where the waters of the river stood and rose up on a heap when Israel crossed over into Canaan; the name means “earth” or “red ground.” Not to be confounded with Adam the first man.
biblical_def: Adam is a city upon the Jordan, beside Zaretan, remembered for one of the great miracles of the conquest — the parting of the river before Israel. As the priests bearing the ark of the covenant dipped their feet in the brim of the flooded Jordan, “the waters which came down from above stood and rose up upon an heap very far from the city Adam, that is beside Zaretan…and the people passed over right against Jericho” (Jos 3:16). The whole river was stopped far upstream at Adam, so that the channel below ran dry, and “the priests that bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the midst of Jordan, and all the Israelites passed over on dry ground” (Jos 3:17). This crossing was the twin of the passage through the Red Sea a generation before: “the LORD your God dried up the waters of Jordan from before you…as the LORD your God did to the Red sea” (Jos 4:23). The city Adam, whose name means earth or ground, marks the very spot where God heaped up the waters to bring His people into their inheritance. It preaches that the same LORD who opened the sea opens the river; no flood, no barrier, no last obstacle can stop the people whom God is determined to bring home. The Jordan of death itself shall part before the ark of His covenant.
webster_summary: A city on the Jordan beside Zaretan where the river’s waters stood on a heap so Israel crossed dry-shod into Canaan; distinct from Adam the first man.
webster_full: ADAM, a city upon the Jordan, beside Zaretan.

corruption_paragraphs: The city Adam faces no postmodern redefinition, though it must be distinguished from Adam the first man. The truth its miracle carries answers the unbelief that reckons the last obstacle too great, the flood too high, the barrier before the promise impassable.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s power to bring His people home. At the city Adam He heaped up the Jordan as He once heaped the Red Sea, and Israel passed over dry. No flood can stop those whom God is determined to bring into their inheritance; the very Jordan of death parts before the ark of His covenant.
